Java Sutra
Java · Interview prep

Three reference sets in one place: object-oriented programming, the Collection Framework, and threads with their methods and states.

OOPs in Java

Object-Oriented Programming is an approach where a program is designed using classes and objects.

Encapsulation

pillar

Wrapping data and methods together in a class and controlling access to the data.

Inheritance

pillar

One class acquires the properties and behavior of another class.

Polymorphism

pillar

One name can have multiple forms.

Abstraction

pillar

Hiding implementation details and showing only essential functionality.

Supporting concepts

ClassObjectConstructorInterfaceAssociationAggregationComposition

Class, object and constructor

Class

blueprint

A class is a blueprint or template for creating objects.

class Student {
    int id;
    String name;

    void display() {
        System.out.println(id + " " + name);
    }
}
  • Student → class
  • id, name → data members
  • display → method

Object

instance

An object is an instance of a class.

Student s = new Student();

s.id = 101;
s.name = "Abhinav";
s.display();
  • Student → class
  • s → reference variable
  • new → creates the object

Constructor

A constructor is a special member used to initialize an object.

class Student {

    Student() {
        System.out.println("Constructor");
    }
}

Student s = new Student();

Default

If you define no constructor, Java provides a default one.

class A {
}

No-argument

A constructor explicitly written without parameters.

class A {
    A() {
        System.out.println("Hello");
    }
}

Parameterized

class Student {

    int id;

    Student(int id) {
        this.id = id;
    }
}

Constructor overloading

Student() {
}

Student(int id) {
}

Student(int id, String name) {
}

Encapsulation

Wrapping data and methods together in a class and controlling access to the data. It is usually achieved with private variables and public getter and setter methods.

class Student {
    private int age;

    public void setAge(int age) {
        this.age = age;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }
}
Data securityData hidingControlled accessEasier maintenance

Inheritance

Inheritance allows one class to acquire the properties and behavior of another class.

class Animal {
    void eat() {
        System.out.println("Eating");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    void bark() {
        System.out.println("Barking");
    }
}

Dog d = new Dog();

d.eat();
d.bark();

Types of inheritance

Single

A
↓
B
class A { }

class B extends A { }

Multilevel

A
↓
B
↓
C
class A { }

class B extends A { }

class C extends B { }

Hierarchical

     A
   /   \
  B     C
class A { }

class B extends A { }

class C extends A { }

Multiple

via interfaces
A   B
 \ /
  C

Java does not support multiple inheritance through classes, but it can be achieved through interfaces.

interface A {
}

interface B {
}

class C implements A, B {
}

Hybrid

via interfaces

A combination of two or more inheritance types. Java doesn't support hybrid inheritance through classes, but interfaces can be used to achieve similar structures.

Polymorphism

Poly means many and morphism means forms. One name can have multiple forms.

Polymorphism
├── Compile-time
└── Runtime

Compile-time

method overloading

Same method name, different parameters.

class Calculator {

    int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    int add(int a, int b, int c) {
        return a + b + c;
    }
}

Overload by changing the number, type or order of parameters:

void show(int a) { }

void show(String a) { }

void show(int a, String b) { }

void show(String a, int b) { }

Runtime

method overriding

A child class provides its own implementation of a parent method.

class Animal {
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Dog barks");
    }
}

Animal a = new Dog();

a.sound();   // Dog barks
Return type alone is not enough. Changing only the return type does not create method overloading, so this does not compile:
int show() {
    return 1;
}

String show() {
    return "Hello";
}

Dynamic method dispatch

The mechanism behind runtime method overriding. The JVM decides at runtime which overridden method executes.

Animal a = new Dog();
a.sound();

Abstraction

Hiding implementation details and showing only essential functionality. Java provides it mainly through an abstract class and an interface.

Abstract class

abstract class Animal {

    abstract void sound();

    void eat() {
        System.out.println("Eating");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {

    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Bark");
    }
}

An abstract class can contain:

  • Abstract methods
  • Concrete methods
  • Variables
  • Constructors
  • Static methods
  • Final methods

Interface

An interface defines a contract that implementing classes must follow.

interface Animal {
    void sound();
}

class Dog implements Animal {

    public void sound() {
        System.out.println("Bark");
    }
}

A class can implement multiple interfaces:

interface A {
}

interface B {
}

class C implements A, B {
}

Methods, this and super

A method is a block of code that performs a specific task.

void display() {
    System.out.println("Hello");
}

Types of methods

Instance

void show() {
}

obj.show();

Called using an object.

Static

static void show() {
}

ClassName.show();

Called using the class.

Abstract

abstract void show();

Has no implementation in the abstract class or interface declaration.

Final

final void show() {
}

Cannot be overridden.

Native

native void show();

Declared with native and implemented outside Java, typically through JNI.

this

current object

Access the current object's variable:

class Student {

    int age;

    Student(int age) {
        this.age = age;
    }
}

Call a current class method, or a current class constructor:

this.show();

this();

super

parent part

super refers to the parent class part of the current object.

super.x;       // parent variable

super.show();  // parent method

super();       // parent constructor

Access modifiers

Java has four access levels.

ModifierSame classSame packageSubclassOther package
privateYesNoNo*No
defaultYesYesYes**No
protectedYesYesYesLimited
publicYesYesYesYes
* A private member isn't directly accessible in a subclass. ** A default (package-private) member is accessible to classes in the same package.

Association, aggregation, composition

Association

relationship

A relationship between two classes. A teacher can be associated with students.

Teacher ───── Student

Aggregation

weak has-a

The teacher can exist independently of the department.

Department
    |
    └── Teacher
class Teacher {
}

class Department {
    Teacher teacher;
}

Composition

strong has-a

The room is considered part of the house.

House
 |
 └── Room
class Room {
}

class House {
    private Room room = new Room();
}

Upcasting and downcasting

Upcasting

automatic

Converting a child reference to a parent reference.

Dog d = new Dog();

Animal a = d;

// or
Animal a = new Dog();

Downcasting

explicit

Converting a parent reference back to a child reference.

Animal a = new Dog();

Dog d = (Dog) a;

Use instanceof when the actual object type isn't certain:

if (a instanceof Dog) {
    Dog d = (Dog) a;
}

Important OOP keywords

KeywordPurpose
classCreate class
objectInstance of class
extendsInherit a class
implementsImplement interface
interfaceDefine interface
abstractDefine abstraction
finalPrevent modification, extension or overriding
thisCurrent object
superParent class
staticClass-level member
privateClass-level access
protectedControlled inheritance or package access
publicAccessible broadly
newCreate object
instanceofCheck object type
object is a concept, not a Java keyword. Java has no object reserved word.

Class→Object→Constructor→Encapsulation→Inheritance→Overloading→Overriding→Abstraction→Abstract Class→Interface→this→super→Access Modifiers→Association / Aggregation / Composition

Java Collection Framework

The Java Collection Framework (JCF) is a set of interfaces, classes and methods used to store and manipulate groups of objects.

Main hierarchy

                    Iterable
                       |
                  Collection
                       |
       ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
       |               |               |
      List             Set            Queue
       |               |               |
  ┌────┼────┐      ┌───┼────┐      ┌───┼────┐
ArrayList LinkedList HashSet TreeSet PriorityQueue
Vector    Stack      LinkedHashSet

Map is separate from Collection

Map
├── HashMap
├── LinkedHashMap
├── TreeMap
├── Hashtable
└── ConcurrentHashMap

Main types

TypeStoresAllows duplicatesOrdering
ListObjectsYesUsually insertion order
SetObjectsNoDepends on implementation
QueueObjectsUsually yesProcessing order
MapKey-value pairsKeys: no Values: yesDepends on implementation

List

List stores elements in a sequence and allows duplicates.

List
├── ArrayList
├── LinkedList
├── Vector
└── Stack

ArrayList

resizable array

Uses a resizable array internally.

ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<>();

list.add("Java");
list.add("Python");

System.out.println(list.get(0));

list.set(1, "C++");

list.remove("Java");

System.out.println(list.contains("C++"));
System.out.println(list.size());
ArrayList<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>();

nums.add(10);
nums.add(20);
nums.add(10);

// Output: [10, 20, 10]
Important methods

LinkedList

doubly linked list

Uses a doubly linked list. It implements List, Deque and Queue.

LinkedList<Integer> list = new LinkedList<>();

list.add(20);
list.addFirst(10);
list.addLast(30);

System.out.println(list);   // [10, 20, 30]
Important methods

Vector

legacy, synchronized

A legacy dynamic-array implementation. It is synchronized.

Vector<Integer> v = new Vector<>();
Important methods

Stack

LIFO

Follows Last In, First Out.

Stack<Integer> stack = new Stack<>();

stack.push(10);
stack.push(20);
stack.push(30);

System.out.println(stack.pop());   // 30
Important methods
For modern Java code, Deque / ArrayDeque is generally preferred over the legacy Stack class.

Set

A Set does not allow duplicate elements.

Set
├── HashSet
├── LinkedHashSet
└── SortedSet
      └── NavigableSet
            └── TreeSet

HashSet

unique, unordered

Stores unique elements and does not guarantee insertion order.

HashSet<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();

set.add(10);
set.add(20);
set.add(10);

System.out.println(set);   // only one 10 is stored
Important methods

LinkedHashSet

insertion order

Maintains insertion order while preventing duplicates.

LinkedHashSet<Integer> set = new LinkedHashSet<>();

set.add(30);
set.add(10);
set.add(20);

System.out.println(set);   // [30, 10, 20]

TreeSet

sorted

Stores unique elements in sorted order.

TreeSet<Integer> set = new TreeSet<>();

set.add(30);
set.add(10);
set.add(20);

System.out.println(set);           // [10, 20, 30]
System.out.println(set.first());
System.out.println(set.last());
Important methods

Queue and Deque

A Queue is generally used to process elements in FIFO order, First In, First Out.

Queue
├── PriorityQueue
└── LinkedList

PriorityQueue

priority order

Processes elements according to their priority or order rather than insertion order.

PriorityQueue<Integer> q = new PriorityQueue<>();

q.add(30);
q.add(10);
q.add(20);

System.out.println(q.poll());   // 10
Important methods

On an empty queue

MethodResult
add()Exception
offer()false
remove()Exception
poll()null
element()Exception
peek()null

Deque

double ended queue

You can insert and remove elements from both ends.

Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
Important methods

ArrayDeque

resizable array

A resizable-array implementation of Deque. It can be used as a stack, a queue, or a deque.

ArrayDeque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();

dq.addFirst(10);
dq.addLast(20);

System.out.println(dq);

Map

Map stores data as key → value. Keys must be unique; values can be duplicated.

Map basics

HashMap<Integer, String> map = new HashMap<>();

map.put(101, "Abhinav");
map.put(102, "Rahul");

// 101 → Abhinav
// 102 → Rahul

HashMap

hashing

Stores key-value pairs using hashing.

HashMap<Integer, String> map = new HashMap<>();

map.put(1, "Java");
map.put(2, "Python");

System.out.println(map.get(1));
System.out.println(map.containsKey(2));

map.remove(2);
Important methods

LinkedHashMap

insertion order

Maintains insertion order. It can also be configured for access-order, which is useful for LRU-style caches.

LinkedHashMap<Integer, String> map = new LinkedHashMap<>();

map.put(3, "C");
map.put(1, "Java");
map.put(2, "Python");

System.out.println(map);

// 3 → C
// 1 → Java
// 2 → Python

TreeMap

sorted keys

Stores keys in sorted order.

TreeMap<Integer, String> map = new TreeMap<>();

map.put(30, "C");
map.put(10, "Java");
map.put(20, "Python");

// keys: 10, 20, 30
Important methods

Hashtable

legacy, synchronized

A legacy synchronized key-value collection.

Hashtable<Integer, String> table = new Hashtable<>();
  • Does not allow null keys.
  • Does not allow null values.
  • Synchronized.
  • Legacy class.

For new code, HashMap or appropriate concurrent collections are generally preferred.

ConcurrentHashMap

multi-threaded

Used when multiple threads need to work with a map concurrently. It is part of java.util.concurrent.

ConcurrentHashMap<Integer, String> map =
        new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

Important collection interfaces

Iterable

Provides:

Collection

Common methods:

List interface

List adds methods such as:

List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();

list.add(10);
list.add(20);
list.add(30);

System.out.println(list.get(1));

list.set(1, 50);

System.out.println(list);

Set interface

Common methods inherited from Collection:

A Set's main purpose is no duplicate elements.

Queue interface

  • offer() → insert
  • poll() → remove
  • peek() → view

Deque interface

push() and pop() make a Deque behave like a stack.

Map interface

Iterator

traverse

Used to traverse a collection.

Iterator<Integer> it = list.iterator();

while (it.hasNext()) {
    System.out.println(it.next());
}

ListIterator

both directions

Works specifically with lists and supports movement in both directions.

ListIterator<Integer> it = list.listIterator();

Comparable and Comparator

Comparable

natural ordering

Used for natural ordering of objects. Main method: compareTo().

class Student implements Comparable<Student> {

    int age;

    public int compareTo(Student s) {
        return this.age - s.age;
    }
}

Comparator

custom ordering

Used for custom ordering. Main method: compare().

Comparator<Student> c = (a, b) ->
        a.age - b.age;
Useful methods

Collections and Arrays utility classes

Don't confuse them. Collection is an interface. Collections is a utility class.

Collections

static methods
Collections.sort(list);
Collections.reverse(list);

Arrays

for arrays
Arrays.sort(arr);

Collection vs Collections

CollectionCollections
InterfaceUtility class
Part of the collection hierarchyContains static utility methods
List, Set, Queue extend itsort(), reverse(), etc.

Types of threads

User thread

default

A normal thread created by the programmer.

class MyThread extends Thread {
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("User Thread");
    }
}

Daemon thread

background

A background thread that supports user threads. It does not keep the JVM alive once all user threads have finished.

MyThread t = new MyThread();
t.setDaemon(true);
t.start();
  • Garbage collection
  • Background monitoring
  • Background services

Ways to create a thread

A. Extend Thread

class A extends Thread {
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Hello");
    }
}

A t = new A();
t.start();

B. Implement Runnable

class A implements Runnable {
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Hello");
    }
}

Thread t = new Thread(new A());
t.start();

C. Lambda

Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
    System.out.println("Hello");
});

t.start();

D. Callable

Callable suits tasks that need to return a result or throw checked exceptions. It is normally used with ExecutorService.

ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
Future<Integer> f = ex.submit(() -> 42);
System.out.println(f.get());
ex.shutdown();

Important thread methods

No method matches that filter.

Priority constants

ConstantValue
Thread.MIN_PRIORITY1
Thread.NORM_PRIORITY5 (default)
Thread.MAX_PRIORITY10

Thread states

A Java thread is in exactly one of six states at any moment, as reported by getState().

StateMeaning
NEWThread created but not started
RUNNABLEReady or running under JVM scheduling
BLOCKEDWaiting to acquire a monitor lock
WAITINGWaiting indefinitely
TIMED_WAITINGWaiting for a specified time
TERMINATEDThread has finished

wait(), notify(), notifyAll()

These are not methods of Thread. They belong to Object, and they matter a great deal in multithreading. They are normally used inside synchronized code.

wait()

Makes a thread wait and releases the object's monitor.

notify()

Wakes one waiting thread.

notifyAll()

Wakes all threads waiting on that object's monitor.

synchronized (obj) {
    obj.wait();
}

Deprecated thread methods

stop(), suspend() and resume() can cause serious synchronization and consistency problems, so they should not be used.

Avoid

stop()
suspend()
resume()

Use instead, as needed

interrupt()
wait() / notify()
ExecutorService
Future
Lock
